title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Sexta — morte morieris phrase / unused sense
pass_a_gloss: I cannot restrain myself from adding a sixth reason to the former ones, drawn first from that phrase by death you shall die: For there exists no place in Scripture that I know, where that phrase to die by death is to be taken of that figured death, which is nothing other than absence of holiness in the soul. Then from the very name of death, which in the Old Testament does not occur to me in that sense, Indeed not even in the New absolutely and without addition, unless perhaps Luke 9:60, leave the dead to bury their dead: in which place yet the Lord does not seem to have looked to the privation of original righteousness common to all, but to unbelief and stubbornness. For since he who does not believe is already condemned John 3:18, and the wrath of God remains upon him John 3:36, nothing prevents calling the unbeliever dead. Grant yet that he looked to that privation, it is solemn for him to transfer words from their proper and commonly used signification to a spiritual and metaphorical one for the sake of covering for a time the light of the Gospel, in which the Apostles ought not to have imitated him. Now who would believe that first law and threat of God, conceived in most usual words by death you shall die, is to be understood in a sense altogether unused, and indeed so that the same word once placed, to be understood once, is taken at once both properly and metaphorically. I could overwhelm you with other arguments, but not all are to be poured out at once and together.
pass_b_english: I cannot help adding a sixth reason to the ones above, drawn first from the phrase 'you shall die the death.' I know no place in Scripture where 'to die the death' is taken of that figured death which is only absence of holiness in the soul. Next, from the name 'death' itself: I do not find that sense in the Old Testament, and not even in the New used absolutely and without addition—unless perhaps Luke 9:60, 'let the dead bury their dead,' where the Lord seems to mean unbelief and stubbornness, not the privation of original righteousness common to all. For whoever does not believe is already condemned (John 3:18), and God's wrath remains on him (John 3:36)—so an unbeliever may well be called dead.

Grant that he meant that privation: it is his way to shift words from their proper, common sense to a spiritual, metaphorical one, to veil the Gospel light for a time—and the Apostles should not have copied him there. Who then believes God's first law and threat, set in the most ordinary words 'you shall die the death,' must be read in a sense wholly unused—and so that the same word, used once and to be taken once, is taken both properly and metaphorically at once? I could bury you with further arguments, but not everything must be poured out at once.
source_text: Temperare mihi non possum quin sextam rationem superioribus adjungam, ductam primum a phrasi illa morte morieris: Nam nullus quod sciam locus extat in scriptura, ubi phrasis illa morte mori de figurata illa morte sit accipienda, quae nihil aliud est quam absentia sanctitatis in anima. Deinde ab ipso nomine mortis, quod in vetere Testamento mihi non occurrit eo sensu, Immo ne in Novo quidem absolute, & sine additamento, nisi forte Luc. ix. 60. sine ut mortui sepeliant suos mortuos: quo tamen loco non videtur Dominus ad privationem originalis justitiae communem omnibus respexisse, sed ad incredulitatem & contumaciam. Cum enim qui non credit jam sit condemnatus Ioh. 3. 18. & super eum ira Dei maneat. Ioh. 3. 36. nihil prohibet incredulum mortuum appellari. Fac tamen eum ad privationem illam respexisse, solemne ei est vocabula transferre a propria & communiter usitata significatione ad spiritualem & metaphoricam lucis Evangelicae ad tempus tegendae causa, in quo eum imitari non debuerunt Apostoli. Iam quis credat primam illam dei legem & comminationem conceptam verbis usitatissimis morte morieris, intelligendam esse sensu prorsus inusitato, & quidem ita ut idem vocabulum semel positum, semel intelligendum, accipiatur simul & proprie, & metaphorice. Possum te obruere aliis argumentis, sed non sunt omnia simul ac semel effundenda.
